CONCERNING THE TRANSFER OF THIRD COUNTRY NATIONALS

The Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica (hereinafter referred to individually as a “Participant” and collectively as the “Participants”),

AFFIRMING their willingness to cooperate concerning the potential transfer of certain third-country nationals present in the United States to Costa Rica,

Have reached the following understandings:

1. Purpose and Scope

The purpose of this Memorandum of Understanding (“MOU”) is to memorialize a non-binding understanding between our Governments to facilitate the transfer of third-country nationals from the United States to Costa Rica.

2. Case-by-Case Consideration and Documentation

2.1. The Government of the United States of America may in its complete discretion propose to the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica the transfer of such third-country nationals, and the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica may in its complete discretion consider accepting such a proposal in whole or in part.

2.2. The Government of the Republic of Costa Rica intends to provide appropriate immigration status or other legal accommodation for third-country nationals transferred consistent with this MOU.

3. Assurances

The Participants intend that all actions taken pursuant to this MOU be in accordance with their respective obligations under: the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, done at Geneva on July 28, 1951; the Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, done at New York on January 31, 1967; the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, adopted in New York on December 10, 1984; and all other relevant international obligations, national constitutions, laws, regulations, and immigration and visa policies, as well as the principle of non-refoulement. Consistent with this intention, the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica assures the Government of the United States of America that it would treat any third-country national transferred from the United States to Costa Rica in a manner that is in accordance with its international legal obligations and that any third-country national

pages.text:
transferred to Costa Rica would not be subjected to persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion, or torture, in Costa Rica, or further transferred to any country in which they would be subjected to persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion, or torture.
4. General Provisions
4.1.The participants intend to develop, to the extent appropriate, operating procedures to assist with implementing this MOU. The Participants intend to consult to resolve any questions about the interpretation or implementation of this MOU.
4.2.Either participant may discontinue its participation in this MOU at any time but, if that should occur, intends to provide written notice to the other participant through diplomatic channels.
4.3.Nothing in this MOU is intended to create any rights or obligations under international or domestic law, including with respect to the disbursement or obligation of funds. All actions undertaken consistent with this MOU are subject to the availability of funds and the applicable laws and regulations of both Participants.
4.4.This MOU becomes operative upon signature by both Participants.

Annex A
Procedures for Transfer of Third-Country Nationals from
the United States to Costa Rica
The participants intend to use the following procedures to implement this arrangement:
1. Individuals eligible to be transferred:
• Individuals eligible for transfer to Costa Rica under this arrangement are nationals of third countries.
• The Government of the Republic of Costa Rica retains the discretion to accept or reject any individual proposed for transfer to Costa Rica.
2. Preliminary number of individuals to be transferred:
• The Government of the United States of America intends to propose for transfer to Costa Rica up to 25 individuals per week.
• The Government of the Republic of Costa Rica may decide to exceed this figure at its discretion and in such case would inform the United States.
3. Procedures for transfer:
• Forty-eight (48) hours before a proposed transfer flight, the Government of the United States of America, via the U.S. Embassy in San Jose, intends to send the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica, the flight manifest of the individuals proposed for transfer.
• In such flight manifests, the Government of the United States of America intends to provide the following information, if available: name; sex; date of birth; nationality; and criminal record, to the extent known to the United States.
• The Government of the Republic of Costa Rica intends to review the flight manifest and indicate its acceptance or rejection of the manifest, or any individual on it, promptly. Any persons not included on the approved manifest are not expected to be allowed on the transfer flight.
• In providing its acceptance of the flight manifest, the Government of the Republic of Costa Rica intends to indicate its preferences for the arrival airport and arrival time for the transfer flight.
• To ensure the safety and security of the transfer flight, the individuals being transferred are expected to be accompanied by appropriate U.S. Department of Homeland Security personnel. The Government of the Republic of Costa Rica intends to facilitate entry for them and the transfer flight crew.
4. Procedures for reception:
• The Government of the Republic of Costa Rica intends that any individuals transferred under this arrangement be received and processed under its relevant immigration laws and procedures.
• The Government of the United States of America expects to compensate the International Organization for Migration (IOM) for services provided to individuals transferred under this arrangement.

Preamble
Charter on Strategic Partnership

Between the Republic of Armenia

and the United States of America
The Republic of Armenia and the United States of America:
1. Affirm the importance of our relationship as friends and strategic  partners. We intend to deepen our partnership to the benefit of both  nations and expand our cooperation across a broad spectrum of  mutual priorities.
2. Emphasize that this cooperation between our two democracies is  based on shared values and common interests. These include  advancing democracy and economic freedom, defending sovereignty  and territorial integrity, strengthening the rule of law and respect for  human rights and fundamental freedoms, supporting innovation and  technological advances, and bolstering energy security.
3. Stress our mutual desire to strengthen our relationship across the  diplomatic, economic, energy, high-tech, educational, scientific,  cultural, legal, defense, and security fields.
Section I: Principles of Partnership
This Charter is based on core basic principles and beliefs shared by both  sides:
1. Support for each other's sovereignty, independence, and territorial  integrity constitute the foundation of our bilateral relations.
2. Our friendship derives from our common commitment to democratic  values and our shared belief that democracy is the chief basis for  political legitimacy and therefore, stability.

This Charter is based on core basic principles and beliefs shared by both sides:

Section II: Economic, Trade, Transport, and Energy Cooperation
Armenia and the United States intend to expand cooperation to enhance job  creation and economic growth, support economic/market reform and  liberalization, promote transport connectivity, improve the bilateral  business climate, and improve market access for goods and services. We  recognize that fair, worker-centered, and sustainable trade is essential to  promoting resilient supply chains, equitable development, freedom, and  prosperity. The United States supports Armenia's efforts to integrate into  the global economy.
1. Acknowledging the importance of increased trade and investment to  economic growth and development, Armenia and the United States  intend to identify strategic opportunities to increase bilateral trade  and investment.
2. Recognizing the importance of a well-functioning, resilient, and secure  market-oriented energy sector, Armenia and the United States intend  to explore opportunities to increase and diversify Armenia's energy  production and supplies. This includes the development of a civil  nuclear power program with the highest standards for nuclear safety,  security, and nonproliferation; efforts to enhance energy security and  efficiency, including through a significant increase in the share of  renewables in Armenia's energy mix; and measures to increase  Armenia's energy connectivity to regional and European markets.
3. Armenia and the United States intend to initiate a working group to  strengthen enforcement of export controls for dual-use goods, align  policy frameworks, and share information. Armenia and the United  States also intend to initiate a joint dialogue on greater access to U.S.  Commerce export-controlled technology by trusted companies  operating in Armenia.

EXPRESSING
 the Participants' interest in establishing a Security alliance for Fugitive Enforcement (SAFE) Task Force in Guatemala to present a means to come together to discuss, share, and collaborate on cases involving the removal of Guatemalan nationals subject to an active warrant in Guatemala.
Have reached the following understandings:
I. PURPOSE
The Participants intend to establish and maintain a Guatemala SAFE Task Force and set forth the scope and principles of cooperation.
II. DEFINITIONS
1.
Guatemala SAFE Task Force
: The coordination team as designated by the Participants encompassing the individual efforts of each unit, division, or agency that integrates institutional objectives while maintaining operational and administrative independence to achieve the goals of this Memorandum of Cooperation (MOC).
2.
Immigration Information
: Information relevant to entries and exits of individuals through legally established border points, as well as the issuance of passports and immigration restrictions. The term includes biographical and biometric information gathered by ERO to assist in the removal of an individual to his/her country of nationality or citizenship, or the transfer to a country as ordered by an immigration judge or other competent authority.
3.
Criminal History
: Information pertaining to a person's previous arrests, warrants, detentions, encounters, and formal charges, as well as convictions recorded by Guatemalan authorities. Learning about the dispositions of such arrests or encounters may require a separate Task Force request to the corresponding judicial municipality providing a resolution or decision issued by courts of justice under the Participants' criminal legal frameworks.
4.
Leads
: Information vetted by Guatemala SAFE Task Force and provided to ERO, which include, but are not limited to, the subject's biographical information, country of citizenship, U.S. address, photographs, and other potential identifying information. Leads may be reactive (e.g., vetted manifests) or proactive (e.g., intelligence-driven).
5.
Request for Information (RFIs)
: Information requests submitted to the Guatemala SAFE Task Force, from ERO via a specific ERO-approved format, which include basic biographical information for the SAFE Task Force to conduct its record checks and provide ERO with any results.
III. SCOPE OF COOPERATION

EXPRESSING the Participants' interest in establishing a Security alliance for Fugitive Enforcement (SAFE) Task Force in Guatemala to present a means to come together to discuss, share, and collaborate on cases involving the removal of Guatemalan nationals subject to an active warrant in Guatemala.

Have reached the following understandings:

I. PURPOSE

The Participants intend to establish and maintain a Guatemala SAFE Task Force and set forth the scope and principles of cooperation.

II. DEFINITIONS

  1. 1. Guatemala SAFE Task Force : The coordination team as designated by the Participants encompassing the individual efforts of each unit, division, or agency that integrates institutional objectives while maintaining operational and administrative independence to achieve the goals of this Memorandum of Cooperation (MOC).
  2. 2. Immigration Information : Information relevant to entries and exits of individuals through legally established border points, as well as the issuance of passports and immigration restrictions. The term includes biographical and biometric information gathered by ERO to assist in the removal of an individual to his/her country of nationality or citizenship, or the transfer to a country as ordered by an immigration judge or other competent authority.
  3. 3. Criminal History : Information pertaining to a person's previous arrests, warrants, detentions, encounters, and formal charges, as well as convictions recorded by Guatemalan authorities. Learning about the dispositions of such arrests or encounters may require a separate Task Force request to the corresponding judicial municipality providing a resolution or decision issued by courts of justice under the Participants' criminal legal frameworks.
  4. 4. Leads : Information vetted by Guatemala SAFE Task Force and provided to ERO, which include, but are not limited to, the subject's biographical information, country of citizenship, U.S. address, photographs, and other potential identifying information. Leads may be reactive (e.g., vetted manifests) or proactive (e.g., intelligence-driven).
  5. 5. Request for Information (RFIs) : Information requests submitted to the Guatemala SAFE Task Force, from ERO via a specific ERO-approved format, which include basic biographical information for the SAFE Task Force to conduct its record checks and provide ERO with any results.

III. SCOPE OF COOPERATION

The Participants intend for the Guatemala SAFE Task Force to facilitate coordination and cooperation within the Participants' investigative purview as it pertains to ERO vetting Guatemalan foreign fugitive leads. The scope of cooperation may include verifying nationality, sharing criminal history information, and confirming warrant information. The Guatemala SAFE Task Force is not intended to replace or preclude other current or future forms of cooperation between the Participants.
IV. PRINCIPLES OF COOPERATION
1. The Participants intend to facilitate cooperation to better identify, locate, and apprehend Guatemalan nationals wanted by Guatemalan law enforcement (i.e., subject to an active warrant(s)); and coordinate the subsequent removal of those who have no legal basis to remain in the United States of America and facilitating access to information that the Guatemala SAFE Task Force intends to utilize to conduct its database checks and confirm warrant information.
a. ERO Guatemala is expected to provide advance notification to Guatemalan authorities of the return of wanted Guatemalans identified as Foreign Fugitive Removals via ICE Air Operations (IAO) charter missions to Guatemala. Through the Guatemala SAFE Task Force, ERO intends to facilitate the transfer of fugitive(s) to Guatemalan authorities' custody upon their arrival in Guatemala, via either an IAO charter mission or commercial flight.
b. PNC is expected to receive and render repatriated fugitives into the appropriate Guatemalan judicial entity's custody according to the procedures and regulations of Guatemalan law.
2. The Participants intend to strengthen their existing cooperation and institutional mechanisms related to law enforcement, technology, data sharing, fingerprint comparison, and communication.
3. Guatemala SAFE Task Force, upon receiving leads or RFIs, is expected to conduct records checks, verify information, and provide results, including sending information to ERO field offices for review and action, as appropriate.
4. The procedures for the identification, search and arrest of subjects with a final order of removal upon arrival in Guatemala and subsequent transfer to Guatemalan authorities as contemplated in this MOC are to be consistent with applicable Guatemalan and United States of America law, regulations, and policies.

5. The Participants intend to strengthen their capabilities through the exchange of best practices, training, and other appropriate means considered necessary or of interest to the Participants.
6. The ERO, through its Guatemala City office, intends to share quarterly reports with the Participants regarding Guatemala SAFE Task Force arrests, lessons learned, and continuation of best practices as it relates to the return of Foreign Fugitive Removals.
7. To strive to make available sufficient personnel, equipment, and other assets to facilitate the scope of cooperation of Guatemala SAFE Task Force, as follows:
a. PNC intends to select personnel from its General Sub Directorate of Criminal Investigations (SGIC) of the National Civil Police to become members of the SAFE Guatemala Task Force based on suitable parameters of stringent professional, psychological, physical, and ethical standards.
b. PNC intends to identify a senior law enforcement officer to serve as the Guatemala SAFE Task Force Coordinator, who is expected to have full responsibility for the day-to-day management of Guatemala SAFE Task Force.
c. ERO, through its Guatemala City office, is expected to provide overall directions (administrative and operational guidance) to the Guatemala SAFE Task Force.
d. The Participants intend for Guatemala SAFE Task Force to be located in a separate facility away from their respective agency locations, based on the availability of funds.
e. ERO is expected to facilitate training and technical assistance to SAFE Guatemala Task Force members, with the goal of enhancing capabilities related to Guatemala SAFE Task Force, to the extent practicable and permitted by the Participants' respective laws and available funding.

1. ERO: The Assistant Director for Removal, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or designee.
2. PNC: The Director of National Civil Police of Guatemala.

Candidates for the PNC liaison staff in the Guatemala SAFE Task Force are expected to undergo regular vetting (including polygraph examinations and human rights or “Leahy and Civilian” vetting) prior to and during the period of their participation in Guatemala SAFE Task Force activities. Any candidate who does not successfully complete the vetting process is expected to be removed from the Guatemala SAFE Task Force immediately.
To remain eligible for participation, the Participants expect that Guatemala SAFE Task Force members are to be vetted and polygraphed annually.

Scope of MOC.
 This MOC describes the general relationships, responsibilities, and understandings for the automated and manual sharing and use of Personal Data in furtherance of the purposes identified in Section 1, paragraph 2 of this MOC.

Purposes for Exchange and Use of Personal Data.
 The Participants intend that this MOC facilitate the exchange and handling of appropriate Personal Data in the interest of national security, public safety, and public security and describes the policies and processes through which such exchanges are intended to occur. Section 2
Definitions
For purposes of this MOC, the following definitions apply:
1.
“Applicable Database(s)”
 means the Automated Biometric Identification System (IDENT), or its successor, including other U.S. datasets available to IDENT or its successor which the U.S. Participant contact point is authorized by applicable national law to disclose to the Belize Participant. Applicable Database(s) also refers to relevant and appropriate biometric databases operated by the Belize Participant and any data in such database which the Belize Participant is authorized to disclose under applicable national law.
2.
“Personal Data”
 means any information through which a person may be identified, directly or indirectly, and includes Biometric Information; associated reference numbers; surnames, first names, former names, other names, aliases, and alternative spelling of names; gender; date and place of birth; current and former nationalities; passport data; data from other identity documents; and criminal, police, and immigration records.
3.
“Biometric Information”
 means data relating to a measurable physical characteristic or personal behavior trait used to recognize the identity or verify the claimed identity of an individual. Examples of Biometric Information include fingerprints, face images, and iris images.
4.
“Processing of Data” or “Process Data”
 means any operation or set of operations which is performed upon Personal Data, including Biometric Information, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, adaptation or alteration, sorting, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission, dissemination or otherwise making available, combination or alignment, blocking, or deleting through erasure or destruction;
5.
“Query” or “Queries”
 means an automated electronic search or searches by the Querying Participant of the Searched Participant’s Applicable Database(s) conducted under this MOC.
6.
“Querying Participant”
 means the Participant that initiates the Query.
7.
“Searched Participant”

Submission of Queries.

Authority to Query.
 The Querying Participant is expected to conduct Queries only when the Querying Participant has authority to do so under its national law and for a purpose described in Section 1, paragraph 2 of this MOC.
3.

 When submitting Queries under this Section, the Querying Participant intends to send to the Searched Participant the following information:

ii. Query metadata, such as date and time stamp, and transaction number; and
iii. Additional Personal Data, including Biometric Information, as may mutually be determined in writing by the Participants.

d. If no match is found, give a notification to this effect to the Querying Participant.

Section 3: Radar and Sensor Data Access and Use
The Participants intend to use the CSII to access and share air, maritime, and ground radar and sensor data with each other and other countries participating in CSII. The Participants intend, through the selective sharing application, to have the ability to select the data they desire to share; however, they intend to maximize this sharing. Each Participant is expected not to share radar and sensor data originating from the other Participant with other countries other than data the other Participant selected expressly for sharing with other countries participating in CSII. The Participants intend to only share air track data via CSII with other countries participating in CSII that are parties to an Aerial Interception Assistance Agreement (AIAA), a Cooperative Nation Information Exchange System Agreement, or other aerial interception instrument with the United States. All data sharing regarding civil aircraft is expected to be done in accordance with the provisions of the CNIES Agreement. This Memorandum of Understanding does not limit a Participant's ability to share its own radar and sensor data with other countries through means other than CSII or other means provided with United States assistance.
To manage the CSII effectively, the United States is expected to have unrestricted access to all data developed through the CSII. The Participants do not intend to charge each other or other countries participating in CSII for use of the data.
Section 4: Radar and Sensor Integration
To increase air, maritime, and ground domain awareness, the Participants may, as mutually approved, integrate El Salvador's radars or sensors into the CSII.
Section 5: Radar and Sensor Integration Equipment
If radars or sensors are integrated into the CSII, the United States may install and use in El Salvador integration equipment, networking equipment, or both for the purpose of sharing data. The United States intends to install integration or network equipment in a manner that does not affect El Salvador's radar or sensor systems.

MEMORANDUM OF COOPERATION
BETWEEN
THE DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY
OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
AND
THE MINISTRY OF INTERIOR OF THE KINGDOM OF BAHRAIN
ON ENHANCING COOPERATION ON BORDER SECURITY
THROUGH THE EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION
The Department of Homeland Security of the United States of America (“DHS”) and the Ministry of Interior of the Kingdom of Bahrain (“MOI”), herein collectively referred to as the “Participants,”
DESIRING
 to cooperate as partners to protect the safety and security of their territories through border, immigration, and traveler screening with a view to denying the entry to their territories to persons who are not eligible for entry, including on terrorism, criminal, or national security grounds;
RECOGNIZING
 a need to exchange biometric and associated data to verify the identity of travelers, applicants for travel authorizations and immigration benefits, migrants, asylum seekers, refugees, and others applying for international protection; to establish their citizenship and immigration status; and to determine whether they have links to terrorism, crimes, or other circumstances rendering them inadmissible or removable, in accordance with the Participants’ respective national law;
RECOGNIZING
 that the exchange of information must occur in a manner that complies with the Participants’ respective human rights obligations, including those relating to privacy and civil and political rights, and acknowledging that the appropriate handling and processing of Personal Data that they share with each other is of critical importance to preserving confidence in the implementation of this Memorandum of Cooperation; and
HAVING REGARD FOR
 United Nations Security Council Resolutions 1373 (2001), 1624 (2005), 2178 (2014), 2322 (2016), and, in particular, 2396 (2017), which decides that Member States shall develop and implement systems to collect biometric data in order to responsibly and properly identify terrorists, in compliance with domestic law and international human rights law, encourages Member States to share such data responsibly, as appropriate, and calls upon them to prevent the movement of terrorists by effective national border controls and controls on issuance of identity papers and travel documents and through measures for preventing counterfeiting, forgery or fraudulent use of identity papers and travel documents;
HAVE REACHED THE FOLLOWING UNDERSTANDINGS:

ON ENHANCING COOPERATION ON BORDER SECURITY
THROUGH THE EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION

The Department of Homeland Security of the United States of America (“DHS”) and the Ministry of Interior of the Kingdom of Bahrain (“MOI”), herein collectively referred to as the “Participants,”

DESIRING to cooperate as partners to protect the safety and security of their territories through border, immigration, and traveler screening with a view to denying the entry to their territories to persons who are not eligible for entry, including on terrorism, criminal, or national security grounds;

RECOGNIZING a need to exchange biometric and associated data to verify the identity of travelers, applicants for travel authorizations and immigration benefits, migrants, asylum seekers, refugees, and others applying for international protection; to establish their citizenship and immigration status; and to determine whether they have links to terrorism, crimes, or other circumstances rendering them inadmissible or removable, in accordance with the Participants’ respective national law;

RECOGNIZING that the exchange of information must occur in a manner that complies with the Participants’ respective human rights obligations, including those relating to privacy and civil and political rights, and acknowledging that the appropriate handling and processing of Personal Data that they share with each other is of critical importance to preserving confidence in the implementation of this Memorandum of Cooperation; and

HAVING REGARD FOR United Nations Security Council Resolutions 1373 (2001), 1624 (2005), 2178 (2014), 2322 (2016), and, in particular, 2396 (2017), which decides that Member States shall develop and implement systems to collect biometric data in order to responsibly and properly identify terrorists, in compliance with domestic law and international human rights law, encourages Member States to share such data responsibly, as appropriate, and calls upon them to prevent the movement of terrorists by effective national border controls and controls on issuance of identity papers and travel documents and through measures for preventing counterfeiting, forgery or fraudulent use of identity papers and travel documents;

HAVE REACHED THE FOLLOWING UNDERSTANDINGS:

Section 1
Purpose and Scope
1.
Scope of Memorandum of Cooperation.
 This Memorandum of Cooperation describes the general terms, relationships, responsibilities, and conditions for the automated and non-automated sharing and use of Personal Data, for the purposes set forth in paragraph 2 of this Section.
2.
Purpose of Memorandum of Cooperation.
 The purpose of this Memorandum of Cooperation is to facilitate the exchange of Personal Data to support the administration and enforcement of the Participants' border security and immigration laws, and to describe the policies and processes through which such exchanges are intended to occur, in order to:
a. Facilitate the screening and vetting of individuals seeking admission or entry at the Participants' borders, applying for travel authorizations, visas or immigration benefits, applying to trusted traveler programs, seeking work-related credentials, or seeking asylum and refugee protection or other forms of international protection;
b. Further the prevention, detection, and investigation of acts that would constitute a crime rendering the individual inadmissible or removable under the laws of either Participant; and
c. Further the prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of serious crime, including terrorism.
Section 2
Definitions
For purposes of this Memorandum of Cooperation, the following definitions apply:
1.
"Applicable Database(s)"
 means:
a. With respect to the DHS: DHS's Automated Biometric Identification System (IDENT) or a successor database;
b. With respect to the MOI: MOI's Abaad System or a successor database.
2.
"Personal Data"
 means any information through which a natural person may be identified, directly or indirectly, and includes biometric data (such as fingerprints, facial images, and iris images); associated reference numbers; surnames, first names, former names, other names, aliases, and alternative spelling of names; gender; date and place of birth; current and former nationalities; passport data; data from other identity documents; and criminal, police, and alien records,
3.
"Processing of Data" or "Process Data"
 means any operation or set of operations which is performed upon Personal Data, whether or not by automated means, such as collection, recording, organization, storage, adaptation or alteration, sorting, retrieval, consultation,

Section 3
Querying of Biometric Data
1.
Information Exchange through Querying.
 For the purposes set forth in Section 1, paragraph 2(a), (b), and (c) of this Memorandum of Cooperation, each Participant intends to provide for the submission of biometric data Queries by the other Participant in order to facilitate the exchange of Personal Data associated with the biometric data.
2.
Authority Required to Query.
 The Querying Participant intends to submit a Query only when it has authority to do so under its applicable national law, regulation, and policy, and only for a purpose described in Section 1, paragraph 2(a), (b), or (c), of this Memorandum of Cooperation.
3.
Query Information Requirements.
 When submitting a Query under this Memorandum of Cooperation, the Querying Participant intends to send to the Searched Participant the following information:
a. Biometric data consistent with the modality parameters set out in paragraph 6 of this Section;
b. A unique reference number that identifies the subject individual and/or the Query;
c. An indicator of the nature of the Querying Participant’s encounter with the individual, including the reason for the Query;
d. Query metadata, such as date and time stamp and transaction number; and
e. When available and authorized by its national law, regulation, and policy:
i. Additional biometric data, which may include iris images and other modalities such as facial images; and
ii. Additional Personal Data that the Participants mutually decide in writing to be relevant.

Section 3
Querying of Biometric Data

  1. 1. Information Exchange through Querying. For the purposes set forth in Section 1, paragraph 2(a), (b), and (c) of this Memorandum of Cooperation, each Participant intends to provide for the submission of biometric data Queries by the other Participant in order to facilitate the exchange of Personal Data associated with the biometric data.
  2. 2. Authority Required to Query. The Querying Participant intends to submit a Query only when it has authority to do so under its applicable national law, regulation, and policy, and only for a purpose described in Section 1, paragraph 2(a), (b), or (c), of this Memorandum of Cooperation.

pages.text:
4.
Responding to Queries.
Upon receipt of a Query, the Searched Participant intends to the  extent permissible under its applicable national law, regulation, and policy:
a. Compare the biometric data transmitted by the Querying Participant against the  Searched Participant's Applicable Database(s);
b. Notify the Querying Participant whether the biometric data provided in the Query  matches biometric data in the Searched Participant's Applicable Database(s) (a  positive match confirmation), unless confirming the match is not shareable under the  Searched Participant's national law, regulation, or policy;
c. Upon confirmation to the Querying Participant of a positive match, make available  to the Querying Participant the Personal Data that is available through the Searched  Participant's Applicable Database(s), to the extent possible and authorized by its  national law, regulation, and policy;
d. If no match is found or confirmation of the match is not shareable under the Searched  Participant's national law, regulation, or policy, give a "no match" notification to the  Querying Participant; and
e. Delete the biometric data included in the Query after:
(i) the Searched Participant has determined whether it has matching biometric data available through its Applicable Database(s);
(ii) if applicable, the Searched Participant has supplied Personal Data from its  systems; and
(iii) if applicable, the Querying Participant has provided information outlined in  paragraph 5 of this Section.
5.
Reciprocal Exchange in Event of a Match.
Should the Searched Participant confirm a  positive match to the Querying Participant as described in paragraph 4 of this Section, the  Searched Participant may also make a request for the reciprocal exchange of Personal  Data. When receiving a request for such a reciprocal exchange, the Querying Participant intends to, to the extent consistent with its national law, regulation, and policy, supply the  Searched Participant with any Personal Data related to the subject individual that the  Querying Participant had available prior to the Query or that it collects during the  encounter that motivated the Query.
6.
Initial

Biometric Modality.
The Participants intend to use fingerprints as the biometric  modality for submitting a Query under this Memorandum of Cooperation. When mutually  decided in writing, the Participants may submit a Query under this Memorandum of  Cooperation using other forms of biometric data, or, until such time as both Participants have a fully operational and automated fingerprint identification system, using other  identifying data, including biographic data.

Imposition of Additional Conditions.
In addition to what is described in this Memorandum  of Cooperation, a Participant supplying Personal Data under paragraph 1 of this Section may impose additional conditions in writing on the use that may be made of such Personal  Data. Such conditions should not include conditions imposed that are unrelated to the  specific facts that gave rise to the unrequested supply of data. or Arrangement for Recurring Sharing.

Section

7

Privacy and

Personal Data Protection
1.
Data Handling Requirements.
Each Participant intends to Process Data consistent with  this Memorandum of Cooperation, and further intends to:
a. Take reasonable steps to ensure that Personal Data is maintained with accuracy,  relevance, timeliness, and completeness as is necessary for lawful processing of the  information, including, where feasible, notifying national contact points if it becomes  aware of significant doubts as to the accuracy, relevance, timeliness, or completeness  of the Personal Data, consistent with Section 8 of this Memorandum of Cooperation; and
b. Retain all Personal Data supplied after a match has been confirmed under this  Memorandum of Cooperation only for so long as necessary for the purpose for which  the Personal Data were supplied or further processed. In any case, neither Participant intends to retain the biometric data to be deleted consistent with Section 3, paragraph  4(e) of this Memorandum of Cooperation, or other Personal Data, beyond the time  limits established by its national law, regulation, and policy.
2.
Information Security.
 The Participants intend to ensure, consistent with Section 9 of this  Memorandum of Cooperation, that they have in place appropriate technical, security and  organizational arrangements for the protection of Personal Data supplied under this  Memorandum of Cooperation.
3.
Sensitive Data.
If a Participant supplies Personal Data that reveals racial or ethnic origin,  political opinions or religious or other beliefs, trade union membership, or Personal Data  concerning health or sexual life, the other Participant intend to Process the Data only under  appropriate safeguards.
4.
Existing Rights Unaffected.
Nothing in this Memorandum of Cooperation is intended to  affect the rights of a data subject, as set out in the applicable Participant's national law,  regulations, and policies, to seek redress for any breach of their data privacy or data  protection in accordance with the applicable Participant's national law.
5.
Notification of Retention Periods.
Each Participant intends to publish or otherwise make  publicly available its data retention periods applicable to Personal Data supplied under this  Memorandum of Cooperation.
6.
Assurances.

7.
Use in Proceedings.
 Consistent with the other paragraphs of this Section, when a  Participant decides to use Personal Data obtained under this Memorandum of Cooperation  in judicial, quasi-judicial, or administrative proceedings consistent with the purposes set  forth in Section 1, paragraph 2, and disclosure of the data may result from such use, the  Participant intending to use the obtained Personal Data in such a proceeding intends to  request and obtain prior written consent from the Participant that provided it and intends to  limit such disclosure to the extent permissible under its applicable national law.

MEMORANDUM OF COOPERATION
BETWEEN
THE DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY
OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
AND
THE MINISTRY OF PUBLIC SECURITY, GOVERNANCE AND
POLICE OF THE REPUBLIC OF COSTA RICA
ON ENHANCING BORDER SECURITY AND PUBLIC SAFETY
COOPERATION
THROUGH THE EXCHANGE OF INFORMATION
The Department of Homeland Security of the United States of America (the “U.S. Participant” or “DHS”) and the Ministry of Public Security, Governance and Police of the Republic of Costa Rica (the “Costa Rican Participant”), herein collectively referred to as the “Participants,”
Having regard for the General Agreement for Economic, Technical, and Related Assistance between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of Costa Rica, signed at San Jose, December 22, 1961, and entered into force September 7, 1962 (hereinafter the “1961 Agreement”).
Desiring to cooperate as partners to protect the safety and security of their States by denying entry to such territories to persons who are not legally eligible for entry, including on terrorism, criminal, or security grounds;
Recognizing a need to have a technical Memorandum of Cooperation (MOC) for the exchange of biometric and associated data for the Biometric Data Sharing Partnership program, including the provision of adequate technology, to verify the identity of travelers, migrants, applicants for immigration benefits, asylum seekers or refugees, to establish their identity, citizenship and immigration status; and to determine whether they are being investigated for, or are suspected, accused, or convicted of, terrorism offenses, administrative violations related to irregular migration, offenses linked to illegal immigration, or crimes rendering them inadmissible or removable, consistent with the Participants’ respective national laws;
Recognizing that the exchange of information is intended to occur in a manner that complies with the Participants’ respective human rights obligations, including those relating to privacy and civil liberties.
Acknowledging that the appropriate handling and Processing of Personal Data that they share with each other is of critical importance to preserving confidence in the implementation of this MOC;

Purpose and Scope
1.
Scope of MOC.
 This objective of this MOC is to specify, in accordance with the Participants' national laws, the general relationships, responsibilities, and understandings of the Participants, and to describe the norms and processes that enable the exchange of Biometric Information and Personal Data, consistent with of the purposes identified in Section 1, paragraph 2 of this MOC.

2.
“Personal Data”
 means any information through which a person may be identified, directly or indirectly, and includes Biometric Information; associated reference numbers; surnames, first names, former names, other names, aliases, and alternative spelling of names; sex; date and place of birth; current and former nationalities; passport data; data from other identity documents; and criminal, police, and alien records.

Responding to Queries.

FRAMEWORK FOR STRATEGIC COOPERATION BETWEEN THE GOVERNMENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA AND THE GOVERNMENT OF THE INDEPENDENT STATE OF PAPUA NEW GUINEA

The Government of the United States of America (the "United States") and the Government of the Independent State of Papua New Guinea ("Papua New Guine,;"), each individually a "Participant" and collectively the "Participants";

Recognizing that the robust and enduring relationship between the Participants is built on a foundation of common values, shared economic and geopolitical priorities, and respect for each Participant's sovereignty;

Considering that the United States and Papua New Guinea have enhanced their defense and security partnership through the Defense Cooperation Agreement and the Agreement Concerning Counter Illicit Transnational Maritime Activity Operations, both of which were signed at Port Moresby on May 22, 2023;

Seeking to realize the full potential of the broader bilateral relationship between the two countries, their businesses, and their people, including through the United States-Papua New Guinea Strategic Partnership Dialogue ("Strategic Partnership Dialogue"), which was held on October 10, 2024;

Acknowledging the desire to establish a strategic framework to outline critical areas of cooperation between the Participants;

Understanding the essential links between cooperation on security, critical minerals and infrastructure, economic and commercial ties, the digital economy, and all other aspects of the Participants' bilateral relationship;

Affirm their intention to cooperate as described in this Framework for Strategic Cooperation (hereinafter referred to as the "Framework"); and

NOW, THEREFORE, the Participants have reached the following understandings:

The Government of the Republic of Guatemala, acting through the Ministry of Government and the Guatemalan Institute of Migration and the Government of the United States of America, acting through the Department of Homeland Security ("DHS"), herein referred to individually as "Participant" and collectively as "Participants,
RECALLING
 the Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Guatemala on Enhancing Cooperation to Prevent and Combat Crime and Other Threats to Public Security, signed in Panama City on August 22, 2019 (hereinafter "MOU");
RECOGNIZING
 that Section 17, paragraph 6 provides that the MOU may be modified with the mutual written consent of the Participants;
Hereby modify the MOU as follows:
Section 3, paragraph 3 of the MOU is modified to read as follows:
"The Participants intend to conduct Queries on third country nationals, particularly those entering or transiting the territory of the Guatemalan Participant, and the Guatemalan Participant intends to conduct Queries on its citizens or nationals who are incarcerated in Guatemala. Aside from Guatemalan citizens or nationals incarcerated in Guatemala, the Participants commit not to conduct Queries on citizens or nationals of the United States of America or Guatemala, provided the individual's nationality is verified through a valid passport or other identification document."
This Modification becomes effective upon the signature of both Participants.
Signed in two originals, in the Spanish and English languages, both texts being equally valid.

El Gobierno de los Estados Unidos de América, actuando a través del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS, por sus siglas en inglés), y el Gobierno de la República de Guatemala, actuando a través del Ministerio de Gobernación y del Instituto Guatemalteco de Migración, en lo sucesivo denominados individualmente como “Participante” y colectivamente como “Participantes”.

MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
BETWEEN
THE GOVERNMENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
AND
THE GOVERNMENT OF THE DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO
CONCERNING AN EXPANDED SECURITY PARTNERSHIP

The Government of the United States of America (hereinafter referred to as the “United States”) and the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (hereinafter referred to as the “DRC”), each a “Participant” and collectively referred to as the “Participants”,

CONSCIOUS of their responsibilities in the areas of peace, security, and defense, in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations and their respective Constitutions;

CONSIDERING the Strategic Partnership Agreement between the United States and the DRC, signed in Washington D.C. on December 4, 2025, by which the United States recognizes the DRC as a strategic Partner expected to play a key role in regional peace, stability, and security;

SEEKING to strengthen the bilateral military and security relationship and promote a durable partnership between the Participants;

RECOGNIZING the need to promote peace, stability, and prosperity in Central Africa and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Great Lakes Region, and to protect the strategic assets and infrastructure located therein against acts of aggression in order to safeguard the Participants’ shared security and defense interests;

AFFIRMING the importance of a lasting strategic partnership based on transparency, accountability, and respect for each of the Participant’s interests;

DESIRING to strengthen military cooperation through existing and future initiatives in order to promote professionalization, interoperability, mutual understanding, and the capacity to respond to such threats;

CONVINCED that cooperation between the Participants is expected to serve their common interests by strengthening defense institutions, ensuring regional security, and fostering mutually beneficial partnerships;

HAVE REACHED THE FOLLOWING UNDERSTANDINGS:

1

pages.text:
SECTION 1: PURPOSE
This security memorandum of understanding (hereinafter referred to as the “Memorandum”) forms part of the Strategic Partnership established between the Participants, through which they recognize each other as strategic partners and seek to strengthen their cooperation in security and defense.
The purpose of this Memorandum is to establish a general framework for cooperation setting out the fundamental and non-exhaustive principles of their bilateral cooperation to promote security, defense, respect for the territorial integrity of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the protection of strategic infrastructure and assets (notably: critical minerals and rare earth elements) and strengthening of national capacities.
It also aims to enable the planning and coordinated implementation of initiatives contributing to the long-term strengthening of national capacities in the security and defense sectors across the DRC, including, where mutually determined, the establishment of facilities, infrastructure, or operational support arrangements.
This Memorandum is intended to guide cooperation while recognizing that the scope, pace, and continuation of activities are subject to the laws, regulations, and strategic assessments of each Participant, to adjust or suspend activities based on progress, resource availability, or changing circumstances.

SECTION 1: PURPOSE

This security memorandum of understanding (hereinafter referred to as the “Memorandum”) forms part of the Strategic Partnership established between the Participants, through which they recognize each other as strategic partners and seek to strengthen their cooperation in security and defense.

The purpose of this Memorandum is to establish a general framework for cooperation setting out the fundamental and non-exhaustive principles of their bilateral cooperation to promote security, defense, respect for the territorial integrity of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the protection of strategic infrastructure and assets (notably: critical minerals and rare earth elements) and strengthening of national capacities.

It also aims to enable the planning and coordinated implementation of initiatives contributing to the long-term strengthening of national capacities in the security and defense sectors across the DRC, including, where mutually determined, the establishment of facilities, infrastructure, or operational support arrangements.

This Memorandum is intended to guide cooperation while recognizing that the scope, pace, and continuation of activities are subject to the laws, regulations, and strategic assessments of each Participant, to adjust or suspend activities based on progress, resource availability, or changing circumstances.

The United States of America (United States) and the Cooperative Republic of Guyana (Guyana) (hereinafter collectively "the Participants"),
HAVING REGARD FOR the need to further develop and advance the long standing relationship of cooperation between the United States and Guyana to address shared security challenges,
HAVE REACHED THE FOLLOWING UNDERSTANDINGS:

1.1 Guyana intends to strengthen counternarcotics cooperation with the United States, including making the necessary human, institutional, legal, technological, and other investments to develop sustainable and effective narcotics interdiction capabilities. 1.2 Guyana intends to improve counternarcotics information-sharing with the United States, including through a Guyana-sponsored and funded Guyana Defence Force Foreign Liaison Officer at the Joint Interagency Task Force South.

Scope.

Purpose and scope

  1. 1. Scope. This Memorandum of Cooperation (herein referred to as “Memorandum”) describes the general relationships, responsibilities, and understandings for the automated and manual sharing and use of appropriate Personal Data, in furtherance of the purposes identified in Section 1, paragraph 2 of this Memorandum.
  2. 2. Purposes for the Exchange and Handling of Data Between Participants. The Participants intend that this Memorandum support the administration and enforcement of the Participants’ respective immigration and border security laws through the exchange and handling of appropriate Personal Data in the interest of national security, public safety, and public security, and describe the policies and processes through which such exchanges are intended to occur. Consistent with the Participants’ respective domestic laws and policies, the Participants intend to exchange information to:
    1. a. Facilitate the screening and vetting, including establishing and verifying identity, of individuals seeking admission, entry, transit or departure at the Participants’ respective national borders, or applying for visas, travel authorizations, or immigration benefits, including applications for trusted traveler programs, work-related credentials, or to seek asylum and refugee protection, or other forms of international protection;
    2. b. Facilitate the determination of whether there are grounds of inadmissibility or removability of an individual under the laws of the United States or Uruguay; or
    3. c. Further the prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of acts that would constitute serious crime, including terrorism, and other acts that would constitute a crime rendering an individual inadmissible or removable under the relevant laws of either Participant, or international law, as applicable.

Section 3

  1. 1. Information Exchange through Querying. For the purposes set forth in Section 1, paragraph 2 of this Memorandum, the Participants intend to allow for the automated submission of biometric Queries to each other’s Applicable Databases to facilitate the lawful and appropriate exchange of other Personal Data and additional information.
  2. 2. Authority Required to Query. The Querying Participant is expected to conduct Queries only when it has authority to do so under its national law and for purposes described in Section 1, paragraph 2 of this Arrangement.
  3. 3. Query Information. When submitting Queries under this Section, the Querying Participant intends to send to the Searched Participant the following information:
    1. a. Biometric information consistent with Paragraph 6 of this Section;
    2. b. A unique reference number that identifies the individual and/or the Query; and when available and authorized by national law and policy:
      1. i. An indicator of the nature of the Querying Participant’s encounter with the individual, including the reason for the Query and information collected or

ii. Query metadata, such as date and time stamp, and transaction number; and
iii. Additional Personal Data and additional information as may mutually be determined in writing by the Participants.
4.
Responding to Queries.
 Upon receipt of the Query, the Searched Participant intends to, on an automated basis and consistent with its applicable national law, regulations, and policy:
a. Compare the biometric information transmitted by the Querying Participant against the Searched Participant's Applicable Database;
b. Notify the Querying Participant through an automated response whether the biometric information provided in the Query matches a record in the Searched Participant's Applicable Database (a positive match confirmation), consistent with applicable national laws and policies;
c. Upon confirmation of a positive match, supply to the Querying Participant relevant Personal Data available through its Applicable Database, as appropriate and to the extent authorized by and consistent with applicable national law and policy;
d. After supplying Personal Data to the Querying Participant, request through the automated querying system Personal Data associated with the matched biometric from the Querying Participant;
e. If no match is found, give an automated notification to this effect to the Querying Participant; and
f. Delete the biometric included in the Querying Participant's Query after it has determined it does not have a matching record or after it has determined it has a matching record available through its Applicable Database and shared the appropriate, associated Personal Data from its systems.
5.
Reciprocal Exchange in Event of a Match.
 Should the procedure referred to in Section 3.4 of this Memorandum show a match to the biometric held by the Searched Participant, the Querying Participant intends to supply the Searched Participant with appropriate Personal Data about the individual that it has collected, or that was generated during the encounter that motivated its original Query, and that was not included in the original Query. The Personal Data supplied under this Paragraph may also include other biometric data when available.

  • a. description of the type of data exchanged;
  • b. the date of exchange;
  • c. the recipient of the Personal Data in case the Personal Data are exchanged with other governmental entities; and
  • d. any applicable Query metadata, including the unique reference number referred to in Section 3, paragraph 3(b) of this Memorandum.

3. Retention of Record. To the extent consistent with applicable national laws, the Participants intend to maintain data recorded under this Section for a period of two (2) years. After this retention period, the Participants intend to immediately delete such recorded data, unless doing so is inconsistent with their national laws and policies, including applicable data protection and retention rules.

Section 11

Transparency

Notwithstanding Sections 7, 8, and 9 of this Memorandum, the Participants do not intend for anything in this Memorandum to be interpreted to interfere with the Participants' obligations under their respective national laws or other applicable arrangements or agreements pertaining to data protection and privacy, which may include obligations to provide individuals with rights and privileges regarding Personal Data.

Section 12

Review

The Participants intend to review the implementation of this Memorandum periodically, including within the first year of operation. As part of such review, the Participants intend to examine the following subjects:

  1. 1. Effectiveness Review. The Participants intend to evaluate the effectiveness of the exchange conducted under this Memorandum in protecting security and public safety as well as the effectiveness of the privacy safeguards applicable to protect the Personal Data exchanged;
  2. 2. Query Review. The Participants intend to review the number and nature of Queries, the number and percentage of matches, and the timeliness of responses;
  3. 3. Case Study Review. The Participants intend to share, to the extent practicable, additional statistics and case studies demonstrating how the exchange of Personal Data under this Memorandum has assisted in identifying criminals, including known or suspected terrorists or other threats to security and public safety, and actions taken as a

Section 13
Expenses
Each Participant is expected to be responsible for its own costs incurred in the implementation of this Memorandum which will be subject to the availability of appropriated funds and other resources at the time of implementation.

Interpretation.

In the event of a discrepancy between the English and Spanish versions of this Memorandum, the Participants intend to clarify such discrepancies in a collaborative manner, but in the event of an irreconcilable discrepancy, the Participants intend that the English version will control.
3.

however, specified 72 COLREGS provisions are not applicable to a vessel of special construction or purpose if the Coast Guard determines that the vessel cannot comply fully with those requirements without interfering with the special function of the vessel.1

The owner, builder, operator, or agent of a special construction or purpose vessel may apply to the Coast Guard District Office in which the vessel is being built or operated for a determination that compliance with alternative requirements is justified,2 and the Chief of the Prevention Division would then issue the applicant a certificate of alternative compliance (COAC) if he or she determines that the vessel cannot comply fully with 72 COLREGS light, shape, and sound signal provisions without interference with the vessel's special function.3 If the Coast Guard issues a COAC, it must publish notice of this action in the Federal Register .4

The Chief of Prevention Division, Southeast District, U.S. Coast Guard, certifies that the M/V ISLA DEL ENCANTO (O.N. 1345510) is a vessel of special construction or purpose, and that, with respect to the positions of the forward and aft masthead lights, it is not possible to comply fully with the requirements of the provisions enumerated in the 72 COLREGS, without interfering with the normal operation, construction, or design of the vessel's car deck. The Chief of Prevention Division, Southeast District, U.S. Coast Guard, further finds and certifies that the lights are configured in closest possible compliance with the applicable provisions of the 72 COLREGS.5

This notice is issued under authority of 33 U.S.C. 1605(c) and 33 CFR 81.18.

Dated: August 20, 2025.

Sarah J. Geoffrion, Captain, U.S. Coast Guard, Chief, Prevention Division, Southeast Coast Guard District.

The Government of the United States of America and the Government of the Republic of Uganda, hereinafter referred to individually as a Party or collectively as the Parties,
DESIRING TO
 ensure the dignified, safe, and timely transfer from the United States of America to the Republic of Uganda of third country nationals present in the United States of America who may seek protection against return to their home country or country of former habitual residence.
AGREE
 as follows:
ARTICLE 1
1. The Government of the United States of America shall in its complete discretion propose to the Government of the Republic of Uganda the transfer of third-country nationals present in the United States of America who may seek protection against return to their home country or country of former habitual residence.
2. The Government of the Republic of Uganda shall in its complete discretion consider accepting in whole or in part a proposal made by the Government of the United States of America in accordance with paragraph 1.
ARTICLE 2
Both Parties' actions under this Agreement shall be in accordance with their obligations under the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, done at Geneva on July 28, 1951; the Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, done at New York on January 31, 1967; the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, adopted in New York on December 10, 1984; and any other respective international obligations, national constitutions, laws, regulations, and immigration and visa policies of the Parties, including consideration by the Government of the Republic of Uganda of requests by these third country nationals for asylum, refugee protection, or equivalent temporary protection.

ARTICLE 3
1. The Government of the Republic of Uganda agrees not to return any person transferred to the Republic of Uganda by the Government of the United States of America to their home country or country of former habitual residence until a final decision has been made regarding any pending protection claims.
2. The Government of the Republic of Uganda shall determine a procedure, consistent with its relevant obligations, to resolve the status of those who may abandon pending claims or fail to seek protection.
3. The Government of the United States of America shall not transfer unaccompanied minors pursuant to this Agreement.
ARTICLE 4
1. The Parties shall develop operating procedures to assist with the implementation of this Agreement.
2. In the event of a conflict of interpretation or implementation, the Parties commit to resolve such matters through dialogue or diplomatic channels.
ARTICLE 5
1. This Agreement shall enter into force upon signature.
2. Either Party may terminate or suspend this Agreement at any time by notifying the other Party in writing.
3. The Parties may agree in writing to any amendments to this Agreement, and such amendments shall constitute an integral part of this Agreement, consistent with any applicable legal requirements.
4. Nothing set forth in this Agreement shall be interpreted in such a way that commits the disbursement or allocation of funds by the Parties. The implementation of this Agreement shall be subject to the availability of funds and technical capacity of each Party.
